correctness.rationale: After scaling to \([-1,1]^3\), orient any cutting plane so its offset is nonnegative; one piece then contains the corresponding central half-cube. Signed coordinate permutations reduce its normal to \(\alpha\ge\beta\ge\gamma\ge0\). The submitted two cases \(\alpha\ge\beta+\gamma\) and \(\alpha<\beta+\gamma\) are exhaustive and each provides an explicit boundary point and cube vertex in the same central half whose squared distance is \(8+(1+t)^2\ge9\). Thus every cut has cost at least three in the scaled cube. A coordinate central cut gives two boxes of side lengths \(1,2,2\), each of diameter three, so scaling back yields \(3/2\). The frozen rational verifier checks the witness formulas on a finite normal grid but is not needed for the universal proof.
correctness.risk: No classification of all optimal planes is proved.

value.rationale: This closes the exact first spatial cube case of the source's minimax-diameter division problem, proving that its natural coordinate upper construction is globally sharp against every plane orientation and offset. The central-half witness is a reusable geometric lower-bound mechanism, not an arbitrary numerical slice.

final_claim: Among all single-hyperplane two-divisions of the unit cube \([0,1]^3\), the minimum possible larger Euclidean diameter of the two pieces is exactly \(3/2\), attained by a coordinate midplane cut.
